name: Iris Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at the Mount Carrow gold mine, an open pit about twenty minutes out of town. My job is the haul roads: I keep them smooth, cambered and watered so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres or slide. I've been on the grader fifteen years and I lead the road crew, three graders and two water carts. The best bit is a fresh road at dawn with the blade cutting clean, and the worst bit is dust storms, when you can't see your own blade.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Paul is a fitter at the same mine, he fixes the trucks I build the roads for. We've got Thomas, who's fourteen, and Grace, who's ten, and a house on Station Street with a mortgage that's about half paid. Sundays are church and then lunch at my mother's, every week, no excuses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years someone from the city tells us the world's about to change, and then we're still out here doing the work. I'd say it after church to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'd be glad. I don't use that AI stuff, I don't trust it, and I'd be happy never to need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Keep grading roads, keep Sunday lunch, keep the kids at the school they're at. We'd keep putting a little aside each week like we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really. Life goes on as it should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever worry about the mine itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, gold goes up and down. But there's twenty years of ore in that hill, the geologists say. That'll see me out, or near enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Paul say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul would say he told me so, because he says computers can't fix a hydraulic leak in the rain. He's very sure of himself, that man.

S0.say: I'd tell people after church that I'm not surprised. Someone from the city is always saying the world's about to change, and we're still out here doing the work.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because I don't use AI, I don't trust it, and I'd be happy never to need it.
S0.do: Keeps grading roads, keeps the kids at their school and keeps Sunday lunch at her mother's. Keeps putting a little aside each week as always.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved that life carries on as it should.
S0.quote: Every few years someone from the city tells us the world's about to change, and then we're still out here doing the work.
S0.fieldNote: Iris is grounded in church, family and the mine's long ore life. She frames tech hype as coming from distant city people. Both she and her husband work at the same mine, which matters later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the companies chasing profits and the tech people pushing it on us. I'd say a good worker is worth more than a machine. I'd say that at work and after church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried, because Paul and I are both at Mount Carrow. If they bring in self-driving trucks, they'll want roads graded by machines too, and robots for maintenance after that. All our eggs are in one basket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more aside, cut the extras, and pray about it. I wouldn't go chasing computer courses, that's not me. I'd talk to Paul about whether one of us should look at the other mine, the one up north, so we're not both at the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a knot in my stomach that doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company offered free training on the new systems, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if they made it part of the job. I wouldn't go looking for it. I'm good at what I do, and I'd rather they valued that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new kitchen we were saving for, and Thomas's trip to the coast with his school. That one would hurt, he's been looking forward to it all year.

S1.say: I'd say at work and after church that it's companies chasing profit and tech people pushing it on us. A good worker is worth more than a machine.
S1.think: Privately I'd be worried because Paul and I both work at Mount Carrow. If trucks drive themselves, graders and maintenance follow, and all our eggs are in one basket.
S1.do: Saves more, cancels the new kitchen and her son's school trip, and prays about it. Avoids seeking computer courses and talks with her husband about one of them moving to another mine.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her stomach that won't go away.
S1.quote: If they bring in self-driving trucks, they'll want roads graded by machines too, and robots for maintenance after that.
S1.fieldNote: Iris's real risk is that both household incomes depend on one mine. She blames companies and tech people and leans on faith and family. She'd only take training if the company built it into the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and it shouldn't be allowed. People need work, it's what gives a life its shape. I'd say the government should stop it, not pay everybody to sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be terrified. If both our jobs go in two years, we've got a few months of savings and half a mortgage. I don't know how we'd keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything, the car payment, the kids' sport, even the money we give at church, I'd hate that. I'd ask my mother if we could move in with her if it came to it. And I'd ask the pastor and the people at church if anyone's got work, any work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like I'm standing on the road and the truck's not stopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government shouldn't pay people to sit at home. If you lost your job, would you take that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it, God forgive me, if it was that or losing the house. I wouldn't be proud of it. But I've got two kids to feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about two years that gives you room to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Two years is nothing. You can't learn a new trade, you can't sell a house in this town quickly, you can't do anything except hold on.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and shouldn't be allowed, because work gives a life its shape. The government should stop it rather than pay everybody to sit at home.
S2.think: Off the record I'd be terrified, because if both our jobs go in two years we've only got a few months of savings and half a mortgage. I don't know how we'd keep the house.
S2.do: Cuts everything, including the car payment, the kids' sport and church giving. Asks her mother about moving in if needed, asks church members for any work, and would take government help to save the house.
S2.feel: Panicked, like standing in the road with a truck that won't stop.
S2.quote: I'd take it, God forgive me, if it was that or losing the house.
S2.fieldNote: The gap between Iris's public stance against handouts and her private willingness to take them was the strongest moment here. She feels out of options because two incomes depend on one mine and she won't retrain quickly. Family and church are her first safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that it's wrong. But I'd also say families need to get ready, because nobody else will do it for us. I'd say it at church, where people listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me 48. I'd still be very scared. I'd want Paul to try to stay on longer, because fitters might last a bit while the robots need fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put every spare dollar on the mortgage, so if the worst happens we owe less. I'd probably stay on the grader until they tell me to go. If Paul can get a course in fixing the new machines, I'd push him to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push Paul to train but not yourself. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paul's good with new things, he likes a gadget. I'm not. Better one of us does it well than both of us do it badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to pay the house down, mostly. With five years the mortgage might be small enough that one wage could carry it. With two, there's no chance.

S3.say: I'd say at church that it's wrong, but that families need to get ready because nobody else will do it for us.
S3.think: At 48 I'd still be very scared. I'd want Paul to stay on longer, because fitters might last a while fixing the robots.
S3.do: Puts every spare dollar onto the mortgage in the first year and stays on the grader until told to go. Pushes her husband to take a course on fixing the new machines while not retraining herself.
S3.feel: Alarmed and often awake at night.
S3.quote: With five years the mortgage might be small enough that one wage could carry it.
S3.fieldNote: Iris's plan with five years is to pay down the house so one wage could carry it, and to bet on her husband's trade. She's open that she won't retrain herself. Her fear stays high because she sees no new path for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it the right way, with apprenticeships and real jobs, not handouts. The mines and the government should be training young people for the work that's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would make me 53. Part of me thinks I could just keep going until then, and maybe retire a bit early. That's probably hoping, but it's what I'd hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, pay the house off as fast as we can, and make sure Thomas gets an apprenticeship in a trade that needs people. Maybe I'd look at a job on the farm side, my brother has sheep. I'd keep the family close, that's what gets you through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can live with it. Ten years is a long time to pray on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't trust AI. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I'd see it more, sure. But I'd still rather a person did the job, and I'd still say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Thomas and Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them close to home, with good jobs and their own families. If that means a trade that a robot can't do, then a trade. I wouldn't want them leaving for the city.

S4.say: I'd say there's time to do it right with apprenticeships and real jobs, not handouts. Mines and the government should train young people for the work that's left.
S4.think: Part of me thinks I could keep going until 53 and maybe retire a bit early. That's probably hoping, but it's what I'd hope.
S4.do: Keeps working and pays the house off as fast as possible. Steers her son into a hands-on trade apprenticeship and considers work on her brother's sheep farm later.
S4.feel: Anxious but able to live with it.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time to pray on it.
S4.fieldNote: Even with a decade, Iris doesn't plan to retrain and hopes to reach an early retirement. Her plans centre on the house, her children's trades and family close by. Her distrust of AI doesn't move with more time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the two years. Paul and I would both be out and there'd be nothing to do but hold on. What would help is the mine keeping people on for the jobs that are left, and proper apprenticeships for grown-ups who want them, not money for nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about church. That's where people would turn first in our town, before any government office. If the government wants to help, it should help those places that already help people.

headlineQuote: Better one of us does it well than both of us do it badly.
portrait: Iris Dubois is a 43-year-old grader operator and road crew lead at the Mount Carrow gold mine, married to a fitter at the same mine, with two children, half a mortgage and a weekly church and family routine. She never uses AI, doesn't trust it, and blames companies and city tech people for pushing it. Her central fear is that both household incomes depend on one mine, which turns the two-year AGI picture into panic and a quiet admission that she would take government help despite opposing handouts. With more time she pays down the house, bets on her husband's trade and her son's apprenticeship, and still doesn't plan to retrain herself.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because she and her husband would both be out of work with nothing to do but hold on.
whatWouldHelp: The mine keeping people on for the jobs that remain, adult apprenticeships for those who want them, and support channelled through churches and community groups that already help.
